title: On the Role of Problem Structure in Single-Layer QAOA
authors: Guilherme Adamatti Bridi, Franklin de Lima Marquezino, Andris Ambainis
abstract: Problem structure is regarded as a key factor influencing the performance of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), yet it remains an informal notion without a precise mathematical characterization. In this work, we address this issue by identifying a mathematical object that captures problem structure as seen from the perspective of the target state amplitude in single-layer QAOA. Specifically, we show that this structure is encoded in a joint probability distribution induced by the unique coarsest partition of the computational basis, determined by problem cost values and mixer-dependent walk counts. The statistical dependence between these classes provides a means of quantifying the available problem structure and identifying necessary conditions for exponential amplification. To assess the extent to which this structure can translate into algorithmic performance, we establish a mean-max non-separation bound relating the parameter-averaged probability of measuring the target configuration to its variational maximum. For NPO-PB problems with polynomially many distinct mixer eigenvalues, these probabilities exhibit the same scaling up to polynomial factors. This allows us to characterize the exponential scaling of optimal amplitude amplification by analyzing the parameter-averaged probability without explicitly optimizing the variational parameters. We then derive an exact expression for the parameter-averaged probability as a matrix inner product involving two objects that separately encode the joint structural distribution and the mixer dynamics. This representation provides a framework for identifying the structural mechanisms governing the amplification of the target-state probability or its exponential suppression relative to the mixer capacity. We demonstrate these mechanisms through analytically tractable examples involving transverse field and Grover mixers.
summary: This work provides a precise mathematical definition for 'problem structure' in the context of QAOA, showing it is encoded in a joint probability distribution derived from the computational basis. The authors establish that the algorithm's performance scaling can be analyzed by examining the parameter-averaged probability, which is expressed as an inner product of structural and mixer dynamics. This offers a powerful tool to diagnose the structural limitations governing quantum optimization.
main_problem: The paper aims to mathematically characterize the vague concept of 'problem structure' as it influences the performance of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA).
main_result: Problem structure is precisely encoded in a joint probability distribution derived from the coarsest partition of the computational basis, allowing for the characterization of amplitude amplification scaling via parameter-averaged probabilities.
method: The authors derive structural bounds and exact expressions for the parameter-averaged probability by relating it to a matrix inner product involving the joint structural distribution and the mixer dynamics.
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on QAOA applied to optimization problems defined by a problem Hamiltonian ($H_C$) and a mixing Hamiltonian ($H_M$) acting on a computational basis Hilbert space.
key_observables: Joint probability distribution ($P^{pzq}_{j,k}$), parameter-averaged measurement probability, structural overlap ($xG_{pzq}^P, M_{pzq}YHS$), and amplitude amplification scaling.
important_parameters: QAOA depth ($p$), variational parameters ($ eta_q, \gamma_q$), and the structural parameters defining the coarsest partition.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on suitable polynomial boundedness assumptions and asymptotic scaling relations for structural overlap.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining the mathematical object for problem structure (the joint probability distribution), then establishing bounds relating average and optimal probabilities, and finally deriving an exact matrix inner product representation to analyze structural mechanisms governing amplification.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous mathematical framework to quantify how the underlying structure of an optimization problem dictates the achievable performance bounds of quantum algorithms like QAOA, which is crucial for understanding the limits of quantum computation.
